claims.text: Increasing FCC/BCC interface coherency enhances the coating's creep resistance.
Increasing the relative volume fraction or density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries enhances creep resistance.
The creep-resistance enhancement arises because FCC/BCC phase boundaries impede dislocation motion under sustained loading.
The starting protective coating is an as-deposited dual-phase HEA containing interspersed FCC and BCC constituents.
The starting coating contains FCC/BCC interfaces with varying coherency.
Controlled deposition and post-deposition annealing can systematically vary FCC/BCC phase fractions and interface coherency.
FCC/BCC phase-boundary coherency and boundary density are the governing structural mediators of creep resistance.
Coherent phase boundaries increase local dislocation pile-up.
Coherent phase boundaries hinder dislocation climb and thereby slow creep deformation.
The proposed barrier effect is enhanced when FCC phase fraction and interface coherency are maximized.
A coating with higher FCC/BCC interface coherency will have a lower creep strain rate and delayed steady-state deformation relative to the baseline.
A coating with a higher FCC phase fraction will have a lower creep strain rate and delayed steady-state deformation relative to the baseline.
The original as-deposited baseline has less coherent phase boundaries than the modified samples.
The hypothesis applies under continuous elevated-temperature creep loading.
Dislocation climb is operative within the proposed loading regime.
Failure to find a statistically significant association between increased interface coherency or FCC fraction and reduced creep rate or delayed steady-state creep would falsify the hypothesis.
